of 1,3-Enynes to Tetra-Substituted CF
3
−Allenyl Ketones

ABSTRACT: The modular four-component carbonylation of
unsaturated hydrocarbons represents an elegant strategy for the
one-pot synthesis of complex carbonyl compounds. However, this
strategy is currently focused on the 1,2-difunctionalization of
olefins or alkynes, and the 1,4-alkylcarbonylation of 1,3-enynes
remains unexplored. In this study, we report a Ni-catalyzed 1,4-
alkylcarbonylation of CF
3
-containing 1,3-enynes under 1 atm of
CO, which affords the tetra-substituted CF
3
-allenyl ketones with
good yields and selectivity. This protocol features mild conditions,
broad substrate scope, and acceptable functional group compati-
bility. Control experiments revealed that the reactivity of oxime esters (regulated by leaving groups) and polarity matching are
crucial for the success of this four-component cascade. Preliminary mechanistic studies suggest that the acyl nickel complex is a key
intermediate in this transformation.
KEYWORDS: 1,4-alkylcarbonylation, nickel catalysis, modular synthesis, alkyl radical, four-component coupling
I
n modern organic synthesis, multicomponent modular
synthesis represents the simplest and most elegant strategy
for the one-step construction of high-value fine chemicals from
cheap bulk chemicals.
1
The widespread occurrence of carbonyl
skeletons in natural products, pharmaceuticals, and polymers
stimulates chemists to develop carbonylative multicomponent
reactions (CMCRs) to access diverse and complex carbonyl
compounds from simple and available starting materials.
2
In
recent years, Wu, Ryu, Beller, and others have reported several
elegant transition-metal (Pd, Co, and Cu) catalyzed, radical-
mediated four-component 1,2-dicarbofunctionalizations of
olefins for the synthesis of ketones, esters, and amides
(Scheme 1a).
3
In contrast, nickel-catalyzed carbonylative
multicomponent reactions (CMCRs) are much less developed,
although Ni catalysis exhibits excellent catalytic properties in
various cross-coupling reactions. This is probably due to the
formation of highly toxic Ni(CO)
4
and Ni(CO)
3
L.
4
On the
other hand, the strong binding affinity of CO to nickel blocks
the interaction between nickel and substrates. In 2019, Zhang’s
group achieved the first Ni-catalyzed carbonylation couplings
of difluoroalkyl bromides with arylboronic acids, which greatly
enriched the radical-mediated carbonylation.
4b
After that,
Zhang’s group successfully extended the Ni catalysis to the
four-component carbonylation coupling of alkenes.
5
In
addition, Wu’s group
6
also developed the nickel-catalyzed
four-component 1,2-carbocarbonylation of olefins with amines
or alcohols. The atmospheric pressure of CO and the broad
nucleophile scope merits made Ni catalysis more attractive
than other metal catalysts. Overall, the four-component
carbonylation reactions have focused on the 1,2-difunctional-
ization of olefins involving fluorinated alkyl radicals (•CF
3
or
•CF
2
COR) and alkoxyalkyl radicals, producing the mono-
carbonyl compounds. In this regard, four-component carbon-
ylation reactions involving the alkyl radicals are less reported,
which may be due to the undesired β-hydrogen elimination,
radical polarity mismatch, and reaction rate incompatibility.
Therefore, it is still highly desirable to develop new modular
four-component carbonylative reactions with inexpensive
transition-metal catalysis and various unsaturated systems as
well as radical precursors under atmospheric pressure of CO.
1,3-Enynes are important building blocks in organic
synthesis, which can serve as the efficient radical acceptors to
undergo 1,2- and 1,4-difunctionalizations.
7
Among them,
Wang’s group
7d
reported a nickel-catalyzed radical 1,4-
dicarbofunctionalization of 1,3-enynes to the fluoroalkylated
allenes, in which the key allenyl-Ni
III
intermediate was formed
by the interaction of Ni
II
species with the allenyl radical
(generated through the tautomerization of the propargyl
radical). Later on, Kong
7h
reported another 1,4-dicarbofunc-
tionalization of 1,3-enynes through the combination of
decatungstate photo-HAT and nickel catalysis. There, a 1,3-
Ni shift pathway was proposed. We envision whether the 1,4-

catalysis under a CO atmosphere (Scheme 1c). One challenge
of this carbonylation reaction is the reactivity problem,
including the possible deactivation of Ni species in the
presence of CO and the short lifetime of allenyl radicals.
8
Another major challenge of this four-component reaction is the
selectivity problem, because there are several competing side
reactions involved, including the direct coupling of alkyl
radicals with nucleophiles,
9
three-component carbonylative
coupling,
10
and three-component coupling without carbon-
ylation
11
(Scheme 1b). Therefore, it is very critical to regulate
the matching performance of the reactivity and selectivity to
achieve this multicomponent carbonylation reaction.
Considering the polarity matching, we elected the CF
3
-
containing 1,3-enyne 1a as the radical acceptor, cyclobutanone
oxime ester
12
2a as the alkyl radical precursor, and phenyl-
boronic acid 3a as the nucleophile to optimize the reaction
conditions with Ni catalysis (Table 1). After many trials, it was
found that the four-component 1,4-alkylcarbonylation of 1,3-
enyne proceeded efficiently to give the desired tetra-
substituted CF
3
-allenyl ketone 4a under Ni catalysis in the
presence of 1 atm of CO pressure. Screening of different nickel
salts showed that Ni(PPh

dioxane was found to be the best one (entries 5−7). It is worth
mentioning that using MTBA as a solvent, the three-
component product 4a′ without CO insertion was obtained
as a single product (entry 5). Various organic and inorganic

The survey of ligands indicated that the
dipyridine-type ligands are uniquely effective (entries 11−13).
Increasing the amount of Et
3
N to 3.0 equiv resulted in a
slightly higher yield of 94% of 4a (entry 14). Finally, control
experiments were performed. In the absence of CO gas, the
three-component 1,4-alkylarylation of 1,3-enyne occurred to
give allene 4a′ in 45% yield (entry 15). In the absence of 1,3-
enyne 1a, the arylcarbonylation of cyclobutanone oxime ester
proceeded smoothly to give ketone 4′′ in 66% yield (entry 16).
These results highlighted the excellent chemoselectivity of this
nickel catalyzed multicomponent cascade. Further investiga-
tion revealed that the nickel catalyst, ligand, and base were all
essential to the success of this four-component reaction (not
shown). It is known that the leaving groups in oxime esters
usually have significant influence on the reaction efficiency.
Therefore, the cyclobutanone oxime esters with different
leaving groups were evaluated (Scheme 2). Replacement of
Boc with F
5
−PhCO, p-CF
3
−PhCO, PhCO, and MeCO
resulted in poor yields of 4a accompanied by the
decomposition of most of the 1,3-enyne. We speculate that
the rate of alkyl radical formation is likely to be different for
cycloketone oxime esters with different leaving groups and that
rate matching is essential for four-component carbonylation
coupling.

With the optimal conditions in hand, the generality and
limitations of various arylboronic acids were first investigated
using 1,3-enyne 1a and oxime ester 2a as the coupling partners
(Scheme 3). Arylboronic acids with electron-withdrawing
groups or electron-donating groups in the para position of
the aromatic ring all reacted well, giving the desired four-
component coupling products 4a-4n in moderate to excellent
yields. A variety of useful functional groups including
trimethylsilyl (4c), bromine (4i), cyan (4j), acetyl (4k),
ester (4l), and trifluoromethyl (4m) survived well under this
nickel catalyst system with satisfactory yields ranging from 74%
to 95%. Remarkably, 4-hydroxyphenylboronic acid was also
amenable, furnishing desired allenyl ketone 4n in 89% yield.
The meta- and multisubstituted arylboronic acids were found
to be the suitable substrates for this transformation (4o-4s).
However, the ortho-substituted substrates failed to give any
desired products, probably due to the steric hindrance effect.
Fortunately, the heterarylboronic acids containing benzofuran
and dibenzothiophene participated well in this reaction, giving
the desired products 4u and 4v in 88% and 87% yields,
respectively. The arylboronic acid masked with naproxen also
gave desired product 4w in 91% yield.
Next, the scope of 1,3-enynes for this nickel-catalyzed
carbonylative multicomponent reaction was investigated. As
shown in Scheme 4, a variety of CF
3
-containing 1,3-enynes
bearing a wide range of functional groups such as cyano (5d),
ester (5e), and halogen (5f and 5i) on the aromatic ring of the
alkyne moiety delivered the corresponding CF
3
-allenyl ketones
in moderate to good yields. The electronic and steric effects of
the alkyne moiety did not show any significant effect on the
reaction efficiency. The 2-naphthyl (5j) and pyridyl (5k) 1,3-
enynes also afforded the desired products in excellent yields.
Notably, 1,3-enyne derived from an aliphatic alkyne also
worked well to give the target product 5l in 90% yield. In
addition to the CF
3
group, ester-modified 1,3-enyne also
provided 47% yield of the target product 5m. To verify the
compatibility of this nickel catalysis with other coupling
partners, a range of alkenes was investigated to realize the 1,2-
alkylcarbonylation. As we expected, an electron-deficient
alkene such as acrylonitrile smoothly participated in the four-
component coupling (5n). Nonactivated alkene and aryl

Encouraged by the fruitful compatibility and functional
group tolerance of arylboronic acids and 1,3-enynes, a variety
of alkyl radical precursors were investigated (Scheme 5). A
range of cyclobutanone oxime esters decorated with phenyl,
benzyl, ester, and amine proceeded efficiently, delivering the
desired products 6a−6e in 70−95% yields. The 3-oxetanone-
derived substrate also provided the desired product 6f in 72%
yield. Unfortunately, the five-membered oxime ester was inert
for this reaction. It is well-known that the alkoxy radical-
mediated C−C bond cleavage is also a powerful strategy for
the generation of the keto-alkyl radicals.
14
We were pleased to
find that various cycloalkyl silyl peroxides are compatible with
this four-component carbonylative reaction after slight
modification of the standard conditions. In particular, less
strained five-, six-, seven-, and 12-membered substrates were
efficient for this transformation and afforded the desired allenyl
ketones 6g-6l in moderate yields. The high regioselectivity of
the C−C bond cleavage is attributed to the favorable formation
of more stable radicals (6m and 6n).
To demonstrate the application potential of this four-
component coupling protocol, the scale-up synthesis and the
derivatizations were carried out, respectively (Scheme 6).
When the model reaction was scaled up to 2.0 mmol, an 83%
yield of 4a was still obtained. Treatment of CF
3
-allenyl ketone
4a with LiAlH
4
at −78 °C afforded valuable CF
3
-allenol 7a in
93% isolated yield. CF
3
-allenol 7a could undergo the Au-
catalyzed cascade hydroxyl elimination and cyclization to give
product 8a in 72% yield. Allenol 7a could also be efficiently
esterified with probenecid (a drug molecule) to afford ester 9a
in 73% yield. In addition, the bromo-containing product 4i
could undergo palladium-catalyzed Suzuki coupling with 1-
cyclopentenylboronic acid to afford product 10i in 91% yield.
To gain further insight into this nickel-catalyzed four-
component coupling, several control experiments were carried
out to elucidate the mechanism. First, a radical trapping
experiment was performed by adding 2.0 equiv of TEMPO to
the model reaction. The reaction was completely inhibited, and
adduct 11 was detected by HRMS, indicating that the reaction
proceeded via an alkyl radical pathway (Scheme 7a).
Replacement of electron-withdrawing group CF

These results showed that polarity matching is very important,
making the addition of the alkyl radical to 1,3-enyne preferable
to the capture of the alkyl radical by nickel (Scheme 7b). To

In conclusion, we have developed a novel Ni-catalyzed 1,4-
alkylcarbonylation of 1,3-enynes under 1 atm of CO. To the
best of our knowledge, this is the first example of four-
component carbonylative coupling of 1,3-enynes. In this
cascade, competitive three-component coupling and carbon-
ylative coupling were successfully avoided by regulating the
reactivity of oxime esters through leaving groups and
controlling the polarity matching of alkyl radicals with 1,3-
enynes. Preliminary mechanistic studies suggest that the acyl
nickel complex is a key intermediate in this transformation.
This one-pot protocol features mild conditions, broad
substrate scope, and excellent functional group compatibility,
thus providing a facile approach to the tetra-substituted CF
3
-
allenyl ketones. This modular synthetic strategy would broaden
the application of carbonylation in organic synthesis.
